newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Govt says Yugo dinar slump over, dinar falls again.
newsitem.headline: Govt says Yugo dinar slump over, dinar falls again.

text.p: Yugoslavia's government has advised the central bank to use part of its forex reserves to support the dinar and prevent it from falling further, a senior government official said on Wednesday.
The dinar plunged to as low as 4.3 to the German mark during the eight-day New Year and Christmas holidays, later to recoup its losses and return to its pre-holiday 3.8 level.
After two days of resting at this level, the dinar resumed its slide on Wednesday to stand at 3.9 to the German mark, street dealers told Reuters.
The National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) launched a set of measures late last week to save the dinar and restore financial discipline over which it lost control in the first days of 1997.
"The NBY will no longer tolerate banks' imbalances. The bank with a zero balance will be prevented from further credit activity," Yugoslav Deputy Prime Minister Jovan Zebic told a news conference.
Zebic said the NBY had intervened on the interbank forex market but had also used part of its scarce hard currency reserves to sell to citizens through commercial banks.
According to the law, Yugoslavs are entitled to buy annually up to 1,000 German marks from commercial banks.
"Banks claim they do not have enough cash to meet the demand. Therefore, they are permitted to sell up to 300 D-marks during the first quarter of 1997," Zebic told journalists.

Zebic acknowledged there were some disturbing movements in the dinar rate during the first days of 1997, but insisted this was due to December payments and increased consumption, along with speculative selling of dinars in the grey economy.
"December is traditionally a month of increasing payments and rising consumption," Zebic said.
He blamed the dinar plunge partly on devaluation fears and disbelief that the official rate was sustainable.
"Even though we have insisted that a devaluation is out of the question for the time being, there was some psychosis and disbelief that the 3.3 rate is sustainable," he said.

Zebic said the key problem was that 60 percent of the M1 money supply, which reportedly stood at 5.6 billion dinars in December, was in circulation and outside the banking system and that many private shops used the holiday period to change dinars into hard currency.
"It is unclear how the central bank could act on the grey economy by imposing measures directed to insolvent commercial banks," an analyst who declined to be named told Reuters.
The analyst said it was a tendency of the Serbian, not the federal, government to produce extremely unrealistic economic targets, which never materialise.
"They have impossible economic targets, and when reality falls short of plans, they get into even deeper trouble and force NBY to print money and cover the gap," the analyst said.
Economists said the whole operation of unwanted monetary expansion took place with the help of some commercial banks, deliberately keeping their balances in the red.

Serbia, its invincibility shaken by more than seven weeks of mass street protest over alleged Socialist vote-rigging, had to pay out overdue salaries and pensions to prevent the risk that political protest might turn into social and economic unrest, analysts said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
